[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Action Pack and the Request Lifecycle in Ruby on Rails"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ruby on Rails is built around the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern, and Action Pack is the core framework that handles the Controller and View layers. Understanding how an HTTP request travels through the Rails stack is essential for building robust applications and debugging complex issues."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Journey of an HTTP Request"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a client sends an HTTP request to a Rails application, it does not hit your controllers immediately. Instead, it passes through a sophisticated middleware pipeline known as Rack, followed by the Action Dispatch router, before finally reaching the Action Controller."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"1. Web Server (Puma/Passenger) receives the TCP connection and passes it to the Rack application."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"2. Rack Middleware Stack processes the request (handling sessions, cookies, CSRF protection, logging)."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"3. Action Dispatch Router matches the URL to a specific controller and action."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"4. Action Controller executes business logic, interacts with models, and renders the view."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Inspecting the Middleware Stack"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can inspect the exact middleware pipeline running in your Rails application by executing the following command in your terminal:"},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"bin/rails middleware"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command outputs the ordered list of Rack middleware components. Each component has the opportunity to inspect, modify, or halt the request before it reaches Action Pack."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Routing and Action Dispatch"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once the request exits the middleware stack, it enters ActionDispatch::Routing. Defined in config/routes.rb, the router inspects the HTTP verb and path to determine the destination."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"Rails.application.routes.draw do
  resources :articles, only: [:index, :show]
end"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"If a user requests GET /articles/5, the router maps this URL to the ArticlesController and invokes the show action, passing parameters such as id: "5" inside the params hash."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Action Controller and the Request Processing"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"ActionController::Base (or ActionController::API for API-only apps) is responsible for processing the request. During this phase, filters (before_action, after_action) execute, parameters are sanitized, and the designated action runs."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"class ArticlesController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_article, only: [:show]

  def show
    # Renders app/views/articles/show.html.erb automatically
  end

  private

  def set_article
    @article = Article.find(params[:id])
  end
end"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"View Rendering and Response"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"After the controller action finishes executing without an explicit redirect or render call, Action Pack automatically triggers the Action View layer. It compiles the corresponding template (ERB, Haml, or JBuilder), injects instance variables defined in the controller, and builds the final HTML or JSON response body."},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Finally, the response travels back up through the Rack middleware stack (allowing headers like cookies and cache controls to be appended), and the web server transmits the HTTP response back to the client."}]
